**Tafsir of Surah "Quraysh"**: it is Makkan according to the majority, and Madani according to al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi. It has four verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿For the familiarity of Quraysh.﴾ (1)

It has been said that this surah is connected in meaning to the one before it. The meaning is: "I destroyed the People of the Elephant for the familiarity of Quraysh," that is, so that Quraysh would be united, or so that Quraysh would be in agreement, or so that Quraysh would be secure and thus keep their two journeys (*rihlatayn*). Among those who counted the two surahs as one was Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and there is no separation between them in his *mushaf*. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "We had an imam who did not separate them, and he would recite them together." 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi said: "We prayed Maghrib behind 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and in the first rak'ah he recited *Wal-tini wal-zaytun* [al-Tin: 1] and in the second *Alam tara kayfa* [al-Fil: 1] and *Li-ilafi Quraysh* [Quraysh: 1]."

Al-Farra' said: "This surah is connected to the first surah [[In al-Farra's book: "Some of them said it was joined to (*Alam tara kayfa fa'ala rabbuka*), etc."]], because He reminded the people of Makkah of His great blessing upon them in what He did to the Abyssinians. Then He said: ﴿For the familiarity of Quraysh﴾, meaning: We did that to the People of the Elephant as a blessing from Us upon Quraysh." The reason is that Quraysh used to go out on their trade, and no one would raid them or approach them in the Jahiliyyah. They would say, "We are the People of the House of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Then the owner of the elephant came to demolish the Ka'bah and take its stones to build with them a house in Yemen for people to perform Hajj to. So Allah destroyed them, and He reminded them of His blessing. That is, Allah made that [happen] for the familiarity of Quraysh, so that they would become accustomed to going out and no one would dare to attack them. This is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas: Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Ali informed me, saying: 'Amir ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, and he was a trustworthy man among the best of people, saying: Khattab ibn Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the familiarity of Quraysh﴾, he said: "My blessing upon Quraysh is their familiarity with the journey of winter and summer." He said: "They used to spend winter in Makkah and summer in al-Ta'if."

According to this view, it is permissible to pause at the ends of verses (*ru'us al-ayy*) even if the sentence is not complete, as we will explain in the course of the surah.

It has also been said: it is not connected, because between the two surahs is ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and that is evidence of the ending of one surah and the beginning of another. And the *lam* is connected to His saying, the Exalted: *li-ya'budu* (let them worship).

That is: let them worship the Lord of this House, for their familiarity with the journey of winter and summer for trade (*li-l-imtar*) [[That is, to bring food.]]. Al-Khalil also said: it is not connected. It is as if he said: "Allah made Quraysh familiar [with it], a familiarity; so let them worship the Lord of this House." The word after the *fa'* acts upon what precedes it, because it is an additional *fa'* that is not conjunctive, like your saying: "Zaydan, so strike [him]." It has also been said: the *lam* in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿For the familiarity of Quraysh﴾ is the *lam* of wonder, meaning: "Marvel at the familiarity of Quraysh." This was said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It has also been said: it means "to" (*ila*).

Ibn 'Amir recited *li-ilafi Quraysh* with a hamzah, shortened (*mukhtalasan*), without a ya'. Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj recited *li-lafi* without a hamzah, seeking lightness. The rest recited *li-ilafi* with a ya', with a hamzah, fully vowelled (*mushba'an*), from *alaftu, u'allifu, ilafan*. The poet said:

*Al-mun'imina idha al-nujumu taghayyarat... wal-zai'inina li-rihlati al-ilaf*

[It is said:] *aliftuhu ilfan wa-ilafan* (I became familiar with it). Abu Ja'far also recited *li-ilfi Quraysh*, and whoever said the two forms combined them, saying:

*Za'amtum anna ikhwatakum Quraysh* [[This is as it stands in the manuscripts of the original, in the nominative as a predicate. In *al-Lisan* and *Sharh al-Qamus*, it is *Quraysha* in the accusative as an apposition.]] ... *lahum ilfun wa-laysa lakum ilaf*

You claim that your brothers are Quraysh; they have *ilf* (familiarity) and you have no *ilaf*.

Al-Jawhari said: "Fulan has become familiar with this place (with kasrah), *yaulafuhu ilfan*, and others made him familiar with it, *alafahu iyyahu*. It is also said: *alaftu al-mawdi' ulifuhu ilafan*. Likewise: *alaftu al-mawdi' ulifuhu mu'alafatan wa-ilafan*, so the form of *af'ala* and *fa'ala* in the past tense became one."

'Ikrimah recited *li-ya'lafa* with a fatha on the *lam*, as an imperative. Likewise it is in the *mushaf* of Ibn Mas'ud. The fatha on the *lam* of the imperative is a dialect mentioned by Ibn Mujahid and others. 'Ikrimah used to criticise those who recited *li-ilaf*.

Some of the people of Makkah recited *ilafi Quraysh* (without the *lam*), citing the statement of Abu Talib, advising his brother Abu Lahab concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

*Fa-la tutrakanna ma hayita li-mu'azzam... wa-kun rajulan dha najdatin wa-'afaf*

*Tazudu al-'idha 'an 'usbatin Hashimiyyatin... ilafuhum fi al-nasi khayru ilaf*

So do not abandon him as long as you live, for one who is honoured; and be a man of courage and chastity. He wards off enemies from a Hashemite band, whose familiarity among the people is the best familiarity.

As for Quraysh, they are the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar. Anyone who is from the offspring of al-Nadr is Qurashi, excluding the Banu Kinanah and those above him. They sometimes say *Qurashi*, and that is the analogical form. The poet said:

*Bi-kulli Qurashiyyin 'alayhi mahabatun*

With every Qurashi upon whom there is awe.

If you mean by Quraysh the tribe (*hayy*), you give it the diptote (*sarafa*) [i.e., you do not apply tanwin]; if you mean by it the clan (*qabilah*), you do not give it *sarf*. The poet said:

*Wa-kafa Quraysh al-ma'dilati wa-sadaha*

[This is the second half of a line by 'Adi ibn al-Raqa' praising al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik. Its first half, as in *al-Lisan*, is:]

*Ghalaba al-masamih al-Walidu sama-hatan*

And the verb *taqarrasha* means to earn, and *taqarrashu* means they gathered together. They had been scattered outside the Haram, so Qusayy ibn Kilab gathered them in the Haram until they took it as a dwelling. The poet said:

*Abuna Qusayyun kana yud'a mujammi'an... bihi jama'a Allahu al-qaba'ila min Fihr*

Our father Qusayy was called "the one who gathers," by him Allah gathered the tribes from Fihr.

It has also been said that Quraysh are the sons of Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr. So whoever was not begotten by Fihr is not Qurashi. The first view is more sound and more established. It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: [We are the offspring of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah; we do not *qafw* (accuse) our mother, and we do not disown our father]. [[*Qafa fulan fulanan*: if he slandered him with what is not in him; that is, we do not accuse her or slander her. It is also said the meaning is: we do not abandon attribution to fathers and attribute ourselves to mothers.]] Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' said: The Prophet ﷺ said: [Indeed Allah chose Kinanah from the offspring of Isma'il, and chose from the Banu Kinanah Quraysh, and chose from Quraysh the Banu Hashim, and chose me from the Banu Hashim]. This is authentic and established; al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated it.

Regarding their being named Quraysh, there are several views. One: because they gathered after dispersal; *taqarrush* means gathering and joining together. Abu Jild al-Yashkuri said: [[It is vowelled in *al-Taj* with a kasrah on the jim.]]

*Ikhwatun qarrashu al-dhunuba 'alayna... fi hadithin min dahrihim wa-qadimi*

Brothers who gathered sins against us, in a matter from their time and from antiquity.

The second: because they were merchants who ate from their earnings. *Taqarrush* is earning, and *qarasha yaqrusu qarshan* means he earned and gathered. Al-Farra' said: "By it Quraysh was named." The third: because they used to search out (*yufattishuna*) the pilgrims (*hajj*, the group of pilgrims) who were in need (*dhu al-khallah*), and they would meet their need. *Al-qarsh* is searching. The poet said:

*Ayyuha al-Shamitu al-muqarrishu 'anna... 'inda 'Amrin fa-hal lahu ibqa'*

[This verse is by al-Harith ibn Hilzah al-Yashkuri in his Mu'allaqah. Its version in *Sharh al-Mu'allaqat* is:]

*Ayyuha al-natequ al-murakkishu 'anna... 'inda 'Amrin wa-hal li-dhaka baqa'*

Al-Tabrizi said: (*al-murakkish*: the one who adorns speech with falsehood so that the king accepts his falsehood. It is said he addresses 'Amr ibn Kulthum with it. The meaning of "wa-hal li-dhaka baqa'" is: falsehood does not endure.) On this version there is no evidence in it.

The fourth: what is narrated that Mu'awiyah asked Ibn 'Abbas why Quraysh was called Quraysh. He said: "After a creature in the sea, one of its strongest creatures, called *al-qirsh*, which eats and is not eaten, and rises and is not risen over." And he recited the saying of Tubba':

*Wa-Quraysh hiya allati taskunu al-bahra... bi-ha summiyat Quraysh Quraysha*

*Ta'kulu al-ratha wal-samina wa-la tatruku... fiha li-dhi janahayni rishsha*

*Hakadha fi al-bilad hayyu Quraysh... ya'kulunal-bilada aklan kamisha*

And Quraysh is the one that dwells in the sea; by it Quraysh was named Quraysh. It eats the rotten and the fat, and leaves in it nothing for any two-winged creature, a feather. Thus in the lands is the tribe of Quraysh, eating the lands with a swift eating. [[That is, quickly.]]

And for them at the end of time is a Prophet, who will cause much killing among them and many wounds. [[*Al-khumush*: plural of *al-khamsh*, which is like *al-khadsh*, occurring in the body and the face.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 106, verse 2:

Mujahid and Humayd read "ilfihim" (إِلْفِهِمْ) with a sukun on the lam and without a ya' (yā'). A similar reading is transmitted from Ibn Kathir. Asma' likewise related that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite "ilfihim." It is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas and others. Abu Ja'far, al-Walid (on the authority of the people of Syria), and Abu Haywa read "ilafihim" (إِلَافِهِمْ) with a hamza, in the mukhtalas manner (a rapid, abbreviated articulation of the vowel), without a ya'. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read "ilafihim" (إيلافهم) with two hamzas, the first kasra and the second sukun. Combining two hamzas in the two words is shadh (anomalous, non-canonical). The rest read "ilafihim" (إِيلافِهِمْ) with a long vowel (madd) and a hamza, and this is the preferred reading. It is a substitute (badal) for the first "ilaf" for clarification (li-l-bayan). It is the verbal noun of "alafa," when you make him "ya'lif" (to accustom or bind by pact). "Alifa" means "ilfan," according to the reading mentioned earlier, meaning: what they had become accustomed to of the journey of winter and summer.

Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid regarding His words, exalted is He: "ilafihim rihlata al-shita' wa-al-sayf," that he said: "The journey of winter and summer does not burden them, as a favour from Him to the Quraysh."

Al-Harawi and others said: The people of the ilaf were four brothers, the sons of Abd Manaf: Hashim, Abd Shams, al-Muttalib and Nawfal. As for Hashim, he used to make a pact (yu'lifu) with the king of Syria, meaning he obtained from him a covenant (habl) and a guarantee (ahd) by which he would be safe in his trade to Syria. His brother Abd Shams used to make a pact with Abyssinia, al-Muttalib with Yemen, and Nawfal with Persia. The meaning of "yu'lifu" is "yujir" (to grant protection). These brothers were therefore called "al-mujirun" (the protectors). The merchants of Quraysh would travel to the cities under the covenant of these brothers, and no one would molest them.

Al-Azhari said: "al-Ilaf" is a comparison of ijara (protection, granting refuge) with khafara (safe-conduct, guarantee).[[In some copies of the original: "al-ijara wa-al-khafara," but we did not find this in al-Azhari's Tahdhib nor in any other lexicographical work. Al-ijara: rescue and protection. Al-khafara (with the kha' having three vowel forms): security.]] It is said: "alafa yu'lifu," when he grants protection to the caravans (hamaʾil) with a khafara. Al-hamaʾil is the plural of hamula.[[Al-hamula (with fatha): the camels that carry loads.]] He said: The interpretation is that the Quraysh were residents of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and had neither crops nor livestock, and they used to obtain provisions (yamirun) in winter and summer in safety, while people were being snatched away around them. So whenever some misfortune befell them, they would say: "We are the people of Allah's Sanctuary," and people would not molest them.

Abu al-Husayn Ahmad ibn Faris ibn Zakariyya mentioned in his tafsir: Sa'id ibn Muhammad related to us, from Bakr ibn Sahl al-Dimyati, with his chain (bi-isnadihi) going back to Ibn Abbas, regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He: "li-ilafi Quraysh, ilafihim rihlata al-shita' wa-al-sayf." The reason is that when hunger (makhmasa) struck one of the Quraysh, he and his dependants would set out to a known place and pitch a tent (khiba') for themselves, and they would die there. Until there came Amr ibn Abd Manaf, who was a chief in his time. He had a son called Asad, who had a close companion (tirb) from the Banu Makhzum, whom he loved and played with. [[Al-tirb (with kasra): the one of the same age, and the one born with you.]] The companion said to him: "Tomorrow we shall perish by i'tifad." Ibn Faris said: This word in this report—I do not know whether it is with a dal or a ra'. If it is with a ra', it may be from al-'afr, meaning dust. If it is with a dal, I do not know its meaning.[[In Lisan al-Arab, under the root '-f-d: al-i'tifad means that a man shuts his door upon himself and does not ask anyone until he dies of hunger.]] Its interpretation, as I think, is that they go to that tent, and die one after another.

He said: So Asad entered upon his mother weeping, and mentioned what his companion had said. He said: So Asad's mother sent to those people with fat and flour, and they lived on it for days. Then his companion came to him again and said: "Tomorrow we shall perish by i'tifad." So Asad entered upon his father weeping, and informed him of his companion's words. This weighed heavily upon Amr ibn Abd Manaf, so he stood up to address the Quraysh, and they used to obey his command. He said: "You have introduced a matter by which you have become few, while the Arabs have multiplied; you have become humbled, while the Arabs have become honoured. You are the people of the Sanctuary of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, the noblest of the children of Adam, and people follow you. This i'tifad is almost reaching you." They said: "We are your followers." He said: "Begin with this man"—meaning the father of Tirb Asad—"and relieve him from i'tifad." They did so. Then he slaughtered the camels (budn), slaughtered rams and goats, then crumbled bread in broth (hashshama al-tharid), and fed the people. Therefore he was named Hashim. In this regard the poet said:

"'Amr, the one who crumbled bread in broth for his people,
while the men of Mecca were stricken by drought (musnitun), gaunt."

[[In Lisan: "'Amr al-'ula..." (the poet's wording).]] [[Musnitun: that is, drought struck them. Al-sana: drought and famine.]]

Then he gathered all the sons of one father into two journeys: in winter to Yemen, and in summer to Syria, for trade. What the rich man profited, he shared with the poor, until their poor became like their rich. Islam came while they were upon this. There were no sons of one father among the Arabs who were wealthier or more honoured than the Quraysh. This is the saying of their poet:

"And those who mingle their poor with their rich,
until their poor become like the sufficient."

They continued thus until Allah sent His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), and He said: "Let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them from hunger with the provision of Hashim, and secured them from fear that the Arabs might multiply and they diminish."

His words, exalted is He: "rihlata al-shita' wa-al-sayf" (rihlata). It is in the accusative by the verbal noun (naṣb bi-l-maṣdar): meaning "irtihalihim rihlatan" (their departure, a journey); or by the fact that "ilafihim" falls upon it; or as an adverb of time (zarf). If you make it in the nominative position (mahall al-raf'), with the meaning "they are the journey of winter and summer," it would be permissible. But the first is preferable. The rihla is the departure (irtihal).

One of the two journeys was to Yemen in winter, because it is a hot land, and the other journey was to Syria in summer, because it is a cold land. Also from Ibn Abbas, he said: They used to spend winter in Mecca for its warmth, and summer in al-Ta'if for its climate. This is among the greatest blessings, that a people have a region of heat that repels the cold of winter, and a region of cold that repels the heat of summer. So Allah, Exalted is He, reminded them of this blessing. The poet said:

"In winter there is a blessing in Mecca,
and its summer in al-Ta'if."

Here there are four issues.

The first: al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi and other scholars chose that His words, exalted is He, "li-ilafi" are connected to what precedes it, and it is not permissible for it to be connected to what follows, which is His words, exalted is He: "fa-l-ya'budu rabba hadha al-bayt" (let them worship the Lord of this House).

He said: If it is established that it is connected to the previous surah—and it has been separated from it by an independent statement, a clarifying resumption, and the line "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful"—then it is clear that it is permissible for readers to pause in recitation before completing the sentence. The stopping points (mawaqif) at which the readers pause are not a transmitted Sunnah from the Prophet (ﷺ); they only intended to teach students the meanings, and once they know them, they may stop wherever they wish. As for pausing when breath runs out, there is no disagreement about it, and one does not repeat what preceded it if this happens to you; rather, start from where your breath stopped you. This is my opinion on it, and there is no evidence for what they said at all. But I adopt the complete pause (al-waqf 'ala al-tamam) out of dislike for departing from them.

I say: From the evidence for the soundness of this is the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Al-hamdu li-llahi rabbi al-'alamin," then he paused; "al-Rahmani al-Rahim," then he paused. This has passed in the introduction of the book.[[See vol. 1, p. 10 onward.]]

The Muslims have agreed that pausing at His words, "ka-'asfin ma'kul" (Al-Fil: 5), is not objectionable. How can it be said that it is objectionable, when this surah is recited in the first rak'a and the one after it in the second rak'a, so there intervenes between them a cessation of recitation with pillars of prayer? No scholar dislikes this. The only reason for disliking it would be that His words, exalted is He, "fa-ja'alahum ka-'asfin ma'kul" is the end of a verse. So by analogy: pausing at the ends of verses should not be prohibited, whether the sentence is complete and the purpose concluded, or not complete and not concluded. Also, the closing rhyme (fawasil) is an adornment and beauty of rhymed speech, and without it the metrical would not be distinguished from prose. There is no doubt that rhymed speech is more beautiful. It is thus established that the fawasil are among the beauties of rhymed speech; whoever makes its fawasil manifest by pausing at them has revealed its beauties, while not pausing hides those beauties and makes prose resemble rhymed speech, and that is a failure to honour what is recited.

The second: Malik said: "Winter is half the year, and summer is half of it." I have always seen Rabi'a ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman [[He is Rabi'a al-Ra'y. He met some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the senior Successors, and he was the authority on fatwa in Medina, and from him Malik ibn Anas and others took knowledge. He died in the year 136 AH.]] and those with him not removing their turbans until the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) rise, which is the nineteenth day of Bashans, and it is the twenty-fifth day of the Roman or Persian reckoning. [[Thus in the originals and in Ibn al-Arabi, that is, of their months.]] He meant by the rising of the Pleiades that the tax collectors (al-su'at) go out, and people move with their livestock to their water-sources, and that the rising of the Pleiades is the beginning of summer and the end of winter. This is something on which there is no disagreement among his companions. Ashhab alone related from him: "When al-Haq'a sets, the night shortens." [[Al-Haq'a: three bright stars close to one another above the shoulder of Orion, and it is one of the lunar mansions.]] So when he made the rising of the Pleiades the beginning of summer, it follows that in the general year there are six months, and then the winter begins after the departure of summer, six months.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam was asked about one who swore not to speak to a man until winter enters. He said: He does not speak to him until seventeen days of Hathur have passed. If he had said "until summer enters," he would not speak to him until seventeen days of Bashans have passed. Al-Qurazi said: As for the mention of this from Muhammad concerning Bashans, it is a slip; it is actually "nineteen days of Bashans," because when you calculate the mansions as they are, with thirteen nights for each mansion, you know that what lies between the nineteenth of Hathur does not end its mansions except by the entry of the nineteenth of Bashans. And Allah knows best.

The third: Some people said: Time has four divisions: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. Others said: it is winter, summer, qayz (midsummer heat), and autumn. What Malik said is more correct, because Allah divided time into two parts [[In the originals: "Because Allah's division of time into two parts, and He did not make a third for them" is not sound. In Ibn al-Arabi: "Because the division of time by Allah into two parts..."]] and did not make a third for them.

The fourth: When Allah, exalted is He, bestowed favour upon the Quraysh with two journeys, winter and summer, as previously mentioned, there is in it evidence for the permissibility of a man conducting his affairs in the two seasons between two places, where his condition in each season is more comfortable than the other, such as sitting in the southern room (al-majlis al-bahri) in summer and in the northern room (al-qibli) in winter; and in making the badhahanjat [[In the book Shifa' al-Alil by al-Shihab al-Khafaji: "al-badhahanj" is an arabicised form of "bad khun" or "bad kir," the air vent in the roof of a house.]] and the khish (reed mats) for cooling, and the lubd (felt) and the yanusa [[In Ibn al-Arabi: "al-yanus." We did not find this root in Arabic lexicons.]] for warmth.

Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to worship Him and to affirm His oneness, on account of their attachment (*ilaf*) to the two journeys. The *fa'* (the particle "then") entered because the sentence carries the sense of a condition, since the meaning is: "If not [for anything else], then let them worship Him for the sake of their attachment [to the journeys]," in the sense that the blessings of Allah upon them are countless. So if they do not worship Him for the rest of His blessings, then let them worship Him for the sake of this one blessing, which is a manifest favour.

"The House" is the Ka'bah (the Sacred House). In defining Himself to them as the Lord of this House, there are two explanations. The first is that they had idols, so He distinguished Himself from them. The second is that through the House they were honoured above the rest of the Arabs, so He mentioned this to them as a reminder of His blessing.

It was also said: "Let them worship the Lord of this House," meaning: let them become accustomed to worshipping the Lord of the Ka'bah, just as they were accustomed to the two journeys.

[[Ikrimah said: The Quraysh had become accustomed to a journey to Busra and a journey to Yemen, so it was said to them: "Let them worship the Lord of this House," meaning: let them remain in Makkah. The journey of winter is to Yemen, and the journey of summer is to Sham.]]

Allah's words: "Who fed them against hunger" — i.e., after hunger. "And made them secure from fear." Ibn 'Abbas said: this was by the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. [[Verse 126, Surah al-Baqarah.]]

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs used to raid one another and take captives from one another, but the Quraysh were safe from this because of that sacred sanctuary (al-Haram). He recited: ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of every thing are brought?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57]. [[Verse 57, Surah al-Qasas.]]

It was also said: the journey in winter and summer was difficult for them, so Allah cast into the hearts of the Abyssinians that they should bring them food by ship. They brought it, and the Quraysh feared them and thought they had come to fight them, so they went out to meet them on guard. When they saw that they had brought food to them and relieved them with provisions, the people of Makkah would go out to Jeddah with camels and donkeys and buy food, a two-night journey away.

It was also said: this feeding was that when they denied the Prophet ﷺ, he invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf." So the famine became severe, and they said: "O Muhammad, invoke Allah for us, for we are believers." He prayed, and Tabalah and Jurash in the land of Yemen became fertile, so they carried food to Makkah, and its people prospered.

Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', Sharik and Sufyan said: "And made them secure from fear" means from fear of leprosy (al-judham), that leprosy would not afflict them in their land.

Al-A'mash said: "And made them secure from fear" means from fear of the Abyssinians with the elephant.

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "And made them secure from fear" means: that the caliphate would be only among them.

It was also said: that is, He spared them the need to take safe-conduct agreements (al-Ilaf) from the kings. And Allah knows best; the wording is general.
